title: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex
description: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipersFigure caption, A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as pro
body: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex with drones and snipersFigure caption, A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in AprilByGrace Eliza GoodwinUpdated 5 hours agoUS President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.Image source, Getty Images"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are. Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month. A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.Image caption, Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles.The Department of Defence declined to provide additional details when reached for comment.Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.

schema.headline: Trump says triumphal arch will be military complex

title: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases
description: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, Prime Ministe
body: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced.Each crown court will be equipped with at least one courtroom dedicated to hearing such cases.They will offer victims private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, and there will be new training for court staff and fixed dates for trials.   Rape Crisis England and Wales welcomed the measures, which are expected to cost around £23m, as a "significant step forward" for the justice system that addressed a number of reforms it had been requesting for many years.          "Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," said the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman.The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech and described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.Under the new measures, to be funded out of the Ministry of Justice budget, court staff will be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first". Earlier this year, the government announced that rape victims would be given access to specialist legal advice throughout the criminal justice process.Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade."For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said. "Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added. "So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said.Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system.She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life.Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him."It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said."It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely."Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials. "The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.  "Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog – not undermine our right to a trial by jury."Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill."I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further."The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

schema.headline: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases

title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US
description: "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted
body: "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference."So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

schema.headline: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US

title: Southampton man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
description: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandA 56-year
body: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandA 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three.Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier.The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The human remains were found at Padstow Walk in Feltham, south-west LondonSheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force said led to more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, more than 300 statements taken and searches of more than 10 addresses and numerous water vessels. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020, two months after she was last seen.An investigation led to a number of arrests on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no-one was charged and the case remained unsolved.Officers previously said she had no fixed address and did not own a vehicle or hold a bank account.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the publicLondon Fire Brigade attended a fire at Bedfont Pits on 5 August that damaged about two hectares of shrubland.The Metropolitan Police said human remains were found by a member of the public at the site near Bedfont Lakes Country Park a week later. Detectives in London handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

schema.headline: Southampton man rearrested after missing mum's remains found

title: Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' at first show since Macklemore controversy in Philadelphia
description: Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes" as he opened his first show since Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestin
body: Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes" as he opened his first show since Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage.The singer began his concert in Philadelphia by addressing the controversy that has since engulfed the tour and prompted all of his support acts to quit."I never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific" and called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable".The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him. The row has seen ticket prices drop and sales decline for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour.Sheeran told the crowd that while he was used to facing criticism for his music, "this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry".He said he wanted to "address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand". "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division", he continued. "But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore."Sheeran said what happened in Israel on 7 October was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain", and what was happening in Gaza was "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate". "My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked."He said he was working out how to contribute in a way that would help "victims of these terrible times - and listening and learning, because I do not know enough".Some protesters waved flags outside the venue, but the concert proceeded largely unfettered.A protester who gave his name as Cooper said he had come out "to support the struggle for" the Palestinian people."We need more people like Macklemore and other artists who have a voice, who have a public platform, to be able to speak on behalf of the Palestinian people and their struggle for liberation, especially in the United States," he said.Of the handful of ticket-holders who stopped to talk to the BBC prior to the show, there was a sentiment of determination to enjoy an evening of music while at the same time supporting freedom of speech.Reacting to Sheeran's remarks as they later left the venue, one fan said he had "covered both sides nicely, and I think everyone leaves happy", while another called his speech "very sincere, and I think that's what the people wanted to hear was sincerity".The controversy began in early September, when Macklemore performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters and referred to the death toll in Gaza as a genocide, a claim Israel rejects. The rapper also said criticism of Israel was not intended as criticism of "my Jewish brothers and sisters".Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Gillette Stadium in Boston, Massachusetts - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed.Billionaire Robert Kraft who owns Gillette Stadium and the American football team the New England Patriots, confirmed he had banned Macklemore from performing during the British singer's forthcoming shows.Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said he was "only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas".Meanwhile, support acts including Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish musician Lukas Graham and his backing band Beoga quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.The artists argued his removal represented a chilling effect on free speech.Do you have tickets? Get in touch by using this link or the form below.

title: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?
description: Image caption, Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buriedByPolitical editorWhen I arrive
body: Image caption, Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buriedByPolitical editorWhen I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library.It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm.That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe?Figure caption, 'There was a lightness in his tone', says Earl Spencer about Charles' reaction to Diana's deathThat's why it was so important to test Earl Spencer's claims. Was he really sure that the then-Prince Charles had sounded "giddy" after his former wife had died on that terrible night in 1997? Both men, after all, were in a moment of profound shock.Did the earl, a historian and former journalist himself, have evidence of another of his memories, that Charles had "hissed" at him that the world would "forget her soon enough"? Why does he, the uncle of William and Harry, think the world needs to hear his version of events from all those years ago?Earl Spencer was resolute; strong in his conviction that his version of events needed to be told as a matter of record. And he recounted his memories of his conversations with the King in meticulous detail, noting carefully in our discussion that the Palace had not explicitly denied his claims, instead choosing to question his judgement.There is deep unhappiness and frustration in Buckingham Palace at what Earl Spencer has put into the public domain. Their strongly worded statement tells you everything you need to know about how upset they are. "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.Bear in mind that the two Charleses have had a difficult relationship for decades. Even before either of them was born, the Spencers and the Windsors, two aristocratic families, had years of splits and spats. In the past 48 hours, allies on either side have lined up to back the two different accounts, with acolytes of the King suggesting he would never have said such things. Others emerged to back Spencer.There is no way of being completely sure what exactly happened. There hasn't been an explicit denial, but the Palace has objected in very strong terms to how Earl Spencer has presented the past. But speaking to Diana's brother for about half an hour, I felt he seemed entirely sure in his own mind. His book is carefully constructed to give his account, as well as pay tribute to his sister's life as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches.Princess Diana: My Sister's StoryWatch the full interview with Laura Kuenssberg.After we had spoken, we walked down to the lake on the estate where, on a wooded island, Diana was laid to rest. It's a place where, Earl Spencer told me, she could be safe from intrusion, and is marked as a burial place with a huge stone urn.We passed the little green rowing boat he uses to go to the island to visit her, and walked to what he calls The Temple. It's an 18th Century building that now bears her name and includes a quote from her and another from his famous eulogy to her. It's a line he now says was specifically intended to be a riposte to the other Charles' suggestion that she would quickly be forgotten: Diana "will never be extinguished from our minds".Earl Spencer told me he was not being "vengeful" and that he was not trying to damage the monarchy - even saying there was more he knew about the King that he could relate but had chosen not to. But by speaking out so boldly, publishing his book, serialising it in the papers, and speaking to us, the earl was not just paying a moving tribute to his sister, but stirring up the long-running contest for control of Diana's memory.Figure caption, Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister DianaIn the closing moments of our interview, Earl Spencer revealed himself not to be a public figure trying to settle old scores or correct myths about his incredibly famous sister. When I asked how much he missed her, he welled up, and nearly three decades on, the tears still came. He said he missed her every day. "The thing with sibling loss? You never get over it," he said.Charles Spencer was a young man when his sister died at 36 in the most awful circumstances. He joked about crying as a 62-year-old man at the end of a TV interview in which he'd discussed the monarchy and also made claims about the King that he was well aware would stir up controversy around the world. In the normally hidden world of Althorp, the grief of a brother was still plainly on display – what happened to Princess Diana is not all in the past.

schema.headline: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?

title: Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost
description: At the end, every fibre of Derek McInnes' being must have wanted to have one of those Steven Gerrard moments, a scream of delight and relief into a Ce
body: At the end, every fibre of Derek McInnes' being must have wanted to have one of those Steven Gerrard moments, a scream of delight and relief into a Celtic Park camera lens, a human reaction to a significant victory on hostile terrain.McInnes, though, showed little emotion. He shook hands with a now beleaguered Martin O'Neill and pretty much got out of there. Later, the first words he uttered on radio were about not going "overboard" after back-to-back wins against their city rivals. "Just three points." he said. "Three points closer to Celtic."That's true, of course, but it was also the first time a Rangers manager has won his first two games against Celtic since Graeme Souness in 1986. McInnes was 15 years old at the time.So there was historical context but also deep relevance in the here and now. Rangers were good, and clearly deserving of the win, but they didn't quite hit the levels of ruthlessness of a week ago at Ibrox. They can be better and yet they won as comfortably as it's possible to win when the margin at the end is just a single goal. Their superiority would have been better reflected had they won by two.O'Neill said there was "not much between the sides" but nobody was really buying that, Celtic folk chief among them. The Celtic manager has problems and they're mounting game-by-game. His team is physically weak and mentally substandard. They have lost the elan they had in a few games in early season. They were out-played, out-muscled and out-coached. Again.O'Neill has time to pause now, time to reassess. Time, perhaps, to question whether he's got the answers to the myriad ills of his team. He doesn't have robust players in midfield because his board has not delivered them. He doesn't have the kind of wingers the club had when Daizen Maeda, Liel Abada, the still unfit Jota and Nicolas Kuhn were knocking around. In Yang Hyun-jun's absence - and week on week he appears to be spoken about as an absent world beater - James Forrest is the best winger they have. So says former captain Scott Brown, who knows Celtic players. Forrest is 35-years-old.Neither does O'Neill, at present, have good instincts. Starting Sebastian Tounekti at Ibrox last week was an odd call and he changed it at half-time. Going with Sam Johnstone in goal at Rangers back-fired. Giving Luke McCowan his first start of the season on Sunday was another curious decision that didn't work. The midfielder was off the pace and never came out for the second half.O'Neill's famed ability to problem-solve and inspire has deserted him, for now. When set against the newfound organisation and vigour of this Rangers set-up then Celtic look jaded. Their supporters are being cast into a scenario that none of them want to be a part of - wondering aloud, or just quietly, if the icon still has it in him. He sounds like he does. If that is the case then he needs more from his assistants - or just better ones. From board level to coaching and playing, the whole operation looks humdrum and in need of a mighty shake. It's as if the 5-1 Champions League disintegration against LASK has removed not just confidence but heart and soul. There was little gumption at Ibrox in the 3-0 League Cup loss, there was only a brief early reaction against Ferencvaros in the Europa League before another beating, and now there's a third poor loss in a row and a fourth inside a month.How quickly things turn. A few short weeks ago, as Rangers exited Europe to the sound of booing, McInnes didn't hold back when assessing the problems in his team.Not a possession team, not a pressing team, not a counter-attacking team, he said. They were also too young and too inexperienced, a collection of individuals but not a unit - no identity, no discernible style of play.What were weaknesses then are, in the blink of an eye, strengths now. Callowness has become youthful excellence. For the second straight week, Olwethu Makhanya was the most dominant and classy defender on the pitch. He's 22. For the second straight week the hardest-working and most effective attacking player was Ryan Naderi. He's 23.Dan Neil and Nico Raskin, aged 24 and 25, were once again hugely influential in the middle of the park. Neil looked fairly ordinary not that long ago. Now he's growing fast as Rangers captain.The oldest Rangers player from the start was James Penrice, who is 27. Celtic had six guys who were older than him in their team. The average age of the line-ups was 26.7 versus 24.4. McInnes has moulded them all into a group of players who have, against Celtic, shown maturity and togetherness. He has really hit on something.Certain things stood out. At half-time, Rangers were not just ahead thanks to Naderi's goal, they were winning battles all over the pitch, just as they had done last Sunday. They were winning aerial duels by 67.6% to 32.4%, they had eight shots to Celtic's one, six on target to Celtic's zero.Camilo Duran had eight touches of the ball, Kevin Kelsy had 13 and Naderi 23. All the individual match-ups were more or less Rangers victories. Even when Celtic's club record-signing Kasper Hogh came on, not a lot changed. Rangers had more chances in the second half.Hogh got no service again, but he's beginning to look like a player so devoid of belief that even if service did come his way there's no guarantee that he'd execute the way he did so often for Bodo-Glimt. When your star striker can't get a start and when your leader, Callum McGregor, is getting over-run, then you have problems, too many for O'Neill to solve.McInnes was right about the three points thing, but the momentum in Glasgow is his now. The energy, the clarity, the optimism is blue and not green. The power has switched with breakneck speed and, of course, it could switch back again if Celtic get their act together.There are massive questions now, though. More than O'Neill would have ever faced in the city before. Rangers look, at the moment, like a club that knows where it wants to go. Celtic, by contrast, look lost in a haze of confusion and uncertainty.

schema.headline: Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost

title: Maddy Cusack: Remember the person, not just the player, family says
description: Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fu
body: Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming"."It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat."They're very difficult days."Olivia and Emily often come to Maddy's memorial bench in Scargill Park in West Hallam, Derbyshire, which is where they all grew up. With both of their birthdays at the end of October, Emily says they'd always planned to spend them together, but "now I just come here"."She used to get us in trouble with my dad when we were younger," she says. "It was always her idea then I'd take the blame for it."In an inquest focusing on darker times in her life, it's this side of Maddy that her family thinks has got lost. Olivia, along with other members of Maddy's family, has campaigned tirelessly since her sister's death, setting up a foundation in her name to support aspiring female footballers. "The foundation keeps me going," she says. "It's been a real lifeline to be able to continue her story."On Saturday, she organised a walk from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United's ground, to near Derby where Maddy lived - a distance of almost 30 miles."The aim with the walk is just to do her proud," Olivia says. "Maddy would love that we were all challenging ourselves."

schema.headline: Maddy Cusack: Remember the person, not just the player, family says

title: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana
description: Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duches
body: Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face."If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied."And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example."I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan. He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997. In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness". His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK.They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK.Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear".Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me".In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m.In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology.Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly worded response to his claims about King Charles.That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life."I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Earl Spencer accused the King of psychological manipulation over the palace's statement."It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the King," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said".Journalist Richard Kay, who had been close friends with Diana, also wrote in the newspaper on Sunday that in the week between her death and funeral, Earl Spencer had told him of a "furious row" with Charles."It was 'about the boys', but he was reluctant to go further," said Kay, adding that Earl Spencer said the then prince had been "utterly pathetic".However, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House on Sunday, Dame Julia Cleverdon, a trusted aide and friend of the King, said the claims about his response to Diana's death did not reflect "the language or the behaviours of a man I've known for 40 years".Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".Dame Julia said: "To say that the Prince of Wales was elated and somehow took any pleasure... he was as if a 10-tonne truck had fallen on him.Her own husband had died a fortnight before Diana and she said Charles "could not have been more supportive, loving, concerned about the children and interested".

schema.headline: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana

title: Danny Dyer among celebrities at water public ownership protest
description: Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry.Activi
body: Actor Danny Dyer, his daughter Dani Dyer and singer Becky Hill have attended a protest in Kent demanding public ownership of the water industry.Activists from Surfers Against Sewage descended on Leysdown on Sunday after 315,000 signed a petition calling for the water industry to be returned to public ownership.Rivals and EastEnders star Dyer, who has been running a caravan park on Isle of Sheppey as part of a new TV series, told the BBC: "Sometimes when you look out to the sea, you can smell the twang in the air."Water UK said that "no sewage spill is ever acceptable", while Southern Water said it was committed to reducing storm overflows.Dyer said that the quality of the water was "a disgrace"."It's a very dangerous thing," he told the BBC.Meanwhile Hill said that she loved swimming in the open water but found it "disgusting" to find human waste in the sea.She said that she was campaigning for her family and other families for a cleaner sea."We can stand up and make a difference," she added.Meanwhile Cliff Roney, a GMB activist who has worked in the water industry for more than 40 years, said: "I have seen this industry at its very best and now at its very worst."If the industry is not brought back into public ownership quickly, we are heading towards a national catastrophe."Water UK said it was working to end sewage spills "as fast as we physically can"."That's why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works," a spokesperson said."This is part of a record £104bn investment programme – the largest in the industry's history – to stop sewage entering our rivers and seas, secure our water supplies and support economic growth."Southern Water's director for environment and innovation, Nick Mills, said its 10-year, £1.5bn Clean Rivers and Seas Plan was "already starting to make a difference"."In Whitstable, we're harnessing both AI and nature-based solutions, and we're investing £90m in improvements to Swalecliffe Wastewater Treatment Works. Together, these measures will dramatically reduce storm overflows in the area."According to Defra's Bathing Water Quality site, the most recent classification for Leysdown is rated good, based on samples taken from 2022 to 2025.There have been no pollution incidents reported there, the website states. title: Richard Hammond thanks 999 crews on Elvington crash anniversary
description: Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly ki
body: Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed.Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show.In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart".In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash.He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die."He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate"."Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said.

schema.headline: Richard Hammond thanks 999 crews on Elvington crash anniversary

title: What we have learned from the Premier League so far as international break looms
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Brighton's 3-0 win over Arsenal could have a big impact on both teams' seasonsByEmlyn BegleyBBC Sport journal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Brighton's 3-0 win over Arsenal could have a big impact on both teams' seasonsByEmlyn BegleyBBC Sport journalistThe Premier League takes a near three-week break as we enter a four-game international window.So, what have we learned from the opening five matches of the season? BBC Sport takes a look.Arsenal are beatableFigure caption, Highlights: Brilliant Brighton batter Arsenal in shock first defeat as championsPremier League champions Arsenal were looking fairly unstoppable in the opening weeks of the season.A win over Brighton on Saturday would have given the Gunners a club-record equalling eighth consecutive win in all competitions to start the season. But that all ended with a 3-0 loss at Amex Stadium on Saturday.The Gunners had not lost a league game by more than one goal, let alone three, since October 2024. It was their heaviest defeat in the league since May 2023 when they lost 3-0 to the same opposition."That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," said boss Mikel Arteta."What we've done, the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable - but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level."Maresca hits ground running at Man CityFigure caption, Man City come out on top in eight goal thriller against SunderlandMany wondered if Manchester City would experience a post-Pep Guardiola slump when the legendary boss left after a decade.Things did not start too well under Enzo Maresca, with the Community Shield defeat by Arsenal.But they have won all five games in the Premier League - and seven in a row in all competitions - after Sunday's entertaining 5-3 win over Sunderland.That takes them three points clear of Arsenal."In the press conference before the game, I said I expect a very tough game," said Maresca. "Then we also conceded two or three goals but we have learned a lot in these eight weeks and this is good."Brighton & Brentford continue to impressFigure caption, Brentford stay unbeaten as they put three past ChelseaBrighton and Brentford, two clubs who have never won a major trophy, have continued to impress this season.Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton enjoyed that 3-0 win over Arsenal to see them sit third in the table, only two points behind the Gunners.Brighton have won at home against the reigning Premier League champions in each of the last three seasons.Star player Pascal Gross laughed and said "no" when BBC Sport asked him if Albion were in the title race. But stranger things have happened...Meanwhile, just one point below them in the table are Keith Andrews' Brentford.Many tipped the Bees to struggle after the departure of Thomas Frank last summer but if anything they improved under their former set-piece coach Andrews.And their start to this season - unbeaten after five games and fourth in the table - is showing he is no one-season wonder as a manager.They go into the break on the back of their most impressive result, a 3-0 home win over Chelsea.Leeds, impressing again under boss Daniel Farke, are also on nine points and in a potential Champions League place.Andoni Iraola's Liverpool and Everton are just below them on goal difference.Carrick under pressure?Figure caption, Cunha's late strike denies Fulham first league win of the seasonSeven years apart, United did the same thing twice hoping for different results - appointing a club legend who last managed in Britain in the Championship after a good start as caretaker boss.In 2019 it was Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and this time it was Michael Carrick.But this season, after Carrick having a summer to work on his team, the Red Devils have only won once in the league.Their five points after five league games is their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season.They go into the international break on the back of a 1-1 draw against Fulham, and even needed a late deflected Matheus Cunha strike to stop the Cottagers winning their first game all season.After the Lisandro Martinez own goal that give Fulham the lead, ex-United captain Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. "Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort."United's owners will have almost three weeks to stew on this before they host fellow underachievers Tottenham (more on them soon) on 10 October.Figure caption, Coventry defeat Forest for first win since Prem returnIn 2024 and 2025, the three promoted teams went straight back down - mostly with really low points tallies too.But that streak came to an end last year when Sunderland finished seventh to qualify for Europe and Leeds came 14th. Only Burnley went down.And the early weeks of this season indicate we could be in for a similar situation.Hull City are eighth after five games, with their 2-1 loss to Newcastle their first defeat.Ipswich are 11th. And Coventry, after losing the first four games without scoring, beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 and only sit in the drop zone on goal difference.No quick fix at SpursFigure caption, Highlights: Villa survive late Spurs scare for first PL win of the seasonTottenham finished 17th the last two seasons, their lowest two finishes since being in the second tier in 1977-78.But expectations were raised after a summer of big spending - with Spurs splashing out £302m as well as making two high-profile loan signings.Defence and midfield in particular were overhauled, with new wingers too.But they are left with one senior striker in Dominic Solanke, who has only scored 12 Premier League goals in over two years at the club."I feel they have overpaid for every player they bought this summer - you can't rule them out from being in and around the relegation battle," said TNT pundit and ex-England international Joe Cole.Saturday's 3-2 loss against Aston Villa sees them sit 19th going into the break - despite scoring their first two league goals of the campaign."We have to put on the pitch something more than we are putting," said manager Roberto de Zerbi."Football is tactical but it is blood, it is fighting, it is first one on the ball. We will suffer until the next game."Chelsea are the great entertainersMany were keen to see what Xabi Alonso could do at Chelsea this season.The Spaniard memorably led Bayer Leverkusen to a historic unbeaten German double in 2023-24.And they made big changes to their squad this summer, with £117m attacking midfielder Morgan Rogers and new first-choice keeper Emiliano Martinez both coming in from Aston Villa.There have been 22 goals in their five league games - more coming against them than for them - and they sit 10th.And that is not even counting the 6-3 win over Leeds in the Carabao Cup.Hugely entertaining for the neutrals - but perhaps not for Chelsea fans or management.

schema.headline: What we have learned from the Premier League so far as international break looms

title: Aleema Khanum: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested
description: The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakist
body: The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said.Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return.The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days.Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media. A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore. Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts". "We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X.Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government."Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings. Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them.Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office. He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated.Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received.While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination.

schema.headline: Aleema Khanum: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested

title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth
description: Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.The podcaster and
body: Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media."Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote. "Oh my goodness – this is so wonderful – welcome River," Susanna Reid said.Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

schema.headline: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth

title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses moral high ground by living in tax exile - Labour Party Chair
description: The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.Speaking t
body: The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do.""Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

schema.headline: Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses moral high ground by living in tax exile - Labour Party Chair
